title: Tax planning after your business crosses $1 million
description: A practical agenda for coordinating the business, the owner's income, and the next stage of growth.
intro: A million dollars in annual sales is a business milestone. It is not a million dollars of taxable profit, and it does not identify the right entity or tax strategy by itself. Start a planning conversation with the economics of the business: operating margin, cash available to the owner, payroll, capital spending, and the owner's other income.

sections.title: Start with the whole picture
sections.text: Create a single view of each entity, its owners, the latest financial statements, and the tax returns already filed. Add an estimate of the current year's results and a cash forecast. A useful plan should explain how a proposed decision affects both the company and the owner, and distinguish a timing benefit from a permanent change in tax cost.

sections.title: Ask for an implementation calendar
sections.text: A recommendation only becomes useful when someone owns the next step. Ask which decisions need a payroll change, which require documentation, which belong in the books, and which require an election or another filing. Set a review date and identify the professional responsible for confirming each requirement.

checklist: Current profit and loss statements and balance sheets for every entity
Prior business and personal returns, with depreciation schedules
Payroll totals, owner payments, loans, and distributions
Planned hiring, purchases, acquisitions, or a possible sale
questions: Which decisions materially change my after-tax cash position?
What assumptions would cause the recommendation to change?
Who will implement and monitor the plan?

title: Revenue, profit, and owner cash are three different numbers
description: Why a seven-figure company can still need a better cash and tax forecast.
intro: Revenue measures sales. Profit reflects the earnings after the expenses included in the relevant financial statement. Cash available to an owner also depends on collections, debt payments, purchases, working capital, and the timing of tax payments. These numbers can move in different directions in the same month.

sections.title: Build a bridge from profit to cash
sections.text: Review receivables, payables, debt principal, capital purchases, inventory, and changes in customer deposits alongside the profit and loss statement. Identify cash committed to payroll and other operating needs before considering an owner withdrawal. A growing business can require more working capital even while reported profit improves.

sections.title: Keep the tax forecast separate
sections.text: Book profit and taxable income can differ. Ask your adviser to identify the adjustments rather than assuming the amount in the accounting software is the amount on the return. A useful dashboard shows operating profit, expected taxable income, and cash available after reserves as separate lines.

checklist: Monthly profit and loss statement and balance sheet
Receivables and payables aging reports
Debt repayment and capital purchase schedule
Rolling cash forecast with an explicit tax reserve
questions: How much of this month's profit has actually been collected?
Which cash payments are not expenses on the income statement?
What amount is available to distribute after operating reserves?

title: When an established owner should review entity structure
description: Bring ownership, operating plans, and owner cash needs into the same conversation.
intro: The entity decision should follow the business, its owners, and its plans. An LLC label alone does not tell you how the business is taxed. A review should consider the legal structure, the federal and state tax treatment, administrative costs, eligibility requirements, and how the owner expects to use the cash.

sections.title: Define the decision before comparing entities
sections.text: Write down whether the business expects to reinvest earnings, distribute cash, bring in investors, add partners, or prepare for an exit. Include the states where the company operates and the owner's expected income from other sources. Ask for a comparison that uses the same operating assumptions for each alternative.

sections.title: Include the cost of changing
sections.text: A proposed entity change can affect payroll, books, contracts, ownership rights, and filings. Ask tax and legal advisers to coordinate the effective date, required steps, and potential consequences. The lowest headline rate is not a complete measure of the owner's result.

checklist: Formation documents and existing tax elections
Ownership percentages and agreements
Projected profit, reinvestment, and distribution needs
Expected investors, acquisitions, or an exit
questions: What is the total company-and-owner result under each option?
Which restrictions apply to the proposed tax treatment?
What does the transition require?

title: An owner compensation review that starts with the work
description: Separate wages, distributions, reimbursements, and loans before making changes.
intro: Owner payments need a clear purpose and consistent records. A salary, a distribution, a reimbursement, and a loan are not interchangeable labels. For an S corporation, the IRS requires reasonable compensation for shareholder services before non-wage distributions are used as a substitute for that compensation.

sections.title: Document responsibilities
sections.text: Describe the owner's duties, time spent, experience, management responsibilities, and the work performed by other employees. Bring payroll records and relevant compensation information to the review. A percentage-of-profit shortcut should not replace an analysis of the services actually provided.

sections.title: Reconcile what the books show
sections.text: Review the payroll ledger, owner distributions, expense reimbursements, and shareholder loan accounts together. Ask the adviser to identify amounts needing correction and explain how those corrections flow into the books and returns. Schedule another review when the owner's role changes materially.

checklist: Owner job description and time commitments
Payroll records and existing wage calculation
Distribution and loan-account activity
Comparable compensation information
questions: What evidence supports the compensation amount?
Do the books distinguish each type of owner payment?
When should we reassess the owner's role?

title: A quarterly tax-planning agenda for growing owners
description: Make the conversation about current results and upcoming decisions.
intro: A quarterly review works best when it starts with updated numbers and ends with decisions, owners, and dates. Bring the year-to-date financial statements, a full-year forecast, payroll information, and a list of decisions likely to happen before the next meeting.

sections.title: Use a current forecast
sections.text: Compare actual results with the assumptions used at the previous meeting. Flag unusual receipts, a major contract, a planned asset purchase, a new location, or an acquisition. Ask the adviser to show how the changed forecast affects the tax-payment plan and the owner's cash needs.

sections.title: Record the decisions
sections.text: Keep a short action register identifying the task, the person responsible, the required documentation, and the target completion date. At the next review, check whether the work happened and whether the facts still support the decision. Separate recommendations from items already implemented.

checklist: Year-to-date financials and updated full-year forecast
Tax payments made and available confirmations
Planned transactions and capital spending
Open implementation items from the previous review
questions: What has changed since the last forecast?
Which decision needs attention before the next meeting?
What documents or approvals are still missing?

title: Build a tax reserve around a forecast, not a guess
description: Coordinate owner income, payment timing, and business cash needs.
intro: A flat percentage of revenue rarely captures an owner's full tax picture. Start with projected taxable income, withholding, payments already made, the entity's tax treatment, and the owner's other income. Ask the adviser to distinguish the estimated final liability from the payments needed during the year.

sections.title: Create a payment map
sections.text: List each payment obligation, the taxpayer making the payment, and the relevant payment channel. Keep evidence of payments where the tax team can find it. The business's payment obligations and the owner's personal obligations should be identified separately.

sections.title: Refresh the forecast when results change
sections.text: A large new contract, weaker margins, an owner distribution, or a major transaction can change the assumptions. Agree on a trigger for revisiting the reserve, rather than waiting until filing time. Keep the operating cash forecast visible so tax payments do not collide with payroll or other commitments.

checklist: Expected business and personal income
Withholding and prior estimated payments
Current cash and working-capital needs
A calendar identifying taxpayer, amount, and review date
questions: Does the reserve reflect profit rather than sales?
Which payment rules apply to each taxpayer?
What event should trigger a new forecast?

title: Make your books useful before asking for a tax strategy
description: A clean handoff reduces avoidable back-and-forth.
intro: Tax planning depends on numbers that the owner and adviser can understand. A reconciled balance sheet is as important as an income statement. Organize transactions so the team can tell what happened, who was paid, what the business acquired, and whether an amount belongs to an owner account.

sections.title: Close the month consistently
sections.text: Reconcile bank and credit-card accounts, review receivables and payables, and identify unresolved transactions. Add schedules for loans, fixed assets, payroll, and owner activity. Record questions as they arise rather than allowing them to accumulate until a filing deadline.

sections.title: Create a repeatable handoff
sections.text: Use the same folder structure and naming convention for each reporting period. Include a short explanation of unusual activity and a list of missing documents. Ask the tax team what additional schedules are needed for the specific business rather than assuming every company needs the same packet.

checklist: Reconciled bank and credit-card accounts
Profit and loss statement and balance sheet
Loan, fixed-asset, payroll, and owner schedules
Supporting invoices and a list of unresolved items
questions: Which balance-sheet accounts are not reconciled?
Who owns the remaining cleanup?
What information is missing from the tax handoff?

title: Build an expense reimbursement process owners can follow
description: Give business expenses a consistent path from receipt to books.
intro: A reimbursement process should tell the person submitting an expense what to provide, where to submit it, and who reviews it. Ask your tax adviser which reimbursement rules apply to the business and the person receiving the payment before adopting a policy.

sections.title: Make the business purpose visible
sections.text: Retain the receipt, identify the business purpose, and record the relevant date and participants when appropriate. Keep business and personal amounts separate. A bank or card statement may show a payment without explaining its purpose or providing all the supporting detail.

sections.title: Connect the policy to the books
sections.text: Assign responsibility for reviewing claims and recording approved payments. Reconcile advances and reimbursements so amounts are not duplicated or left in an unexplained account. Ask the adviser to confirm the policy's substantiation and timing requirements for the actual arrangement.

checklist: Written submission and review process
Receipts and documented business purpose
Clear treatment of advances and personal portions
A reconciliation between claims, payments, and the ledger
questions: Which reimbursement arrangement applies here?
What evidence and timing are required?
Who checks that the expense is recorded only once?

title: Plan the equipment purchase before choosing its tax treatment
description: Keep operational need, financing, and tax timing in one model.
intro: An equipment purchase is first an operating and cash decision. List the asset's purpose, expected use, financing terms, delivery schedule, and the date it will be ready for business use. Ask the adviser to evaluate the applicable tax treatment with those facts rather than assuming a purchase automatically creates a particular deduction.

sections.title: Compare the full cash cost
sections.text: Include down payments, debt service, maintenance, training, installation, and any working-capital effect. Separate the cash forecast from the expense recognized in the books and the deduction expected on the return. The three schedules may have different timing.

sections.title: Maintain the asset record
sections.text: Keep purchase agreements, invoices, financing documents, and information about business use. Ask which elections, classifications, and placed-in-service records the tax team needs. Discuss the potential effect of later sale or disposal before treating the initial deduction as the whole outcome.

checklist: Asset description, invoice, and financing terms
Delivery, installation, and business-use records
Expected operating benefit and total cash cost
Existing fixed-asset and depreciation schedules
questions: When will the asset be placed in service?
Which treatments are available under the actual facts?
What happens if the asset is sold later?

title: Prepare for a retirement-plan design conversation
description: Start with the owner, the workforce, and the company's cash commitments.
intro: Retirement-plan design is a company decision that includes employees as well as owners. Prepare workforce information, compensation records, existing plan documents, and a realistic view of the business's ability to fund contributions. A contribution goal by itself is not a plan design.

sections.title: Bring the workforce facts
sections.text: Ask the plan professional which employee information is required for eligibility and design analysis. Include expected hiring, compensation changes, and any related businesses. Coordinate the discussion among the tax adviser, plan administrator, and investment professional so assumptions are shared.

sections.title: Ask about ongoing obligations
sections.text: Understand administration, testing, funding, reporting, and employee communication before choosing a plan. Ask for an annual calendar and a named person responsible for each task. Model a weaker-profit year as well as the current year so recurring commitments are visible.

checklist: Employee census prepared for the plan professional
Owner and employee compensation information
Existing plans and related-business information
Contribution budget and an ongoing administration calendar
questions: How does the design affect eligible employees?
What costs and annual obligations accompany it?
Can the business support the commitments in a lower-profit year?

title: Tax questions to ask before buying another business
description: Organize the diligence conversation before signing the transaction documents.
intro: Before buying a business, define what is being purchased and which advisers are responsible for the tax, legal, and financial review. The headline purchase price does not explain the treatment of assets, liabilities, owner interests, or future payments.

sections.title: Reconcile the operating story
sections.text: Compare financial statements, tax returns, bank activity, payroll, and the seller's supporting schedules. Identify adjustments that are proposed rather than proven. Ask who will investigate discrepancies and what information must be resolved before a decision.

sections.title: Model the transaction structure
sections.text: Ask the transaction team to compare the proposed structure, allocation, financing, contingent payments, and expected post-closing cash flow. Include integration costs and the buyer's ability to operate the business after closing. Keep the purchase documents and the tax model consistent.

checklist: Proposed transaction structure and purchase agreement
Financial statements, returns, and supporting schedules
Asset, debt, payroll, and ownership records
Financing terms and post-closing cash forecast
questions: What exactly are we buying?
Which tax assumptions depend on the final agreement?
What obligations might remain after closing?

title: A year-end planning checklist for established owners
description: Bring the decisions forward while there is still time to act.
intro: A useful year-end review distinguishes decisions still available from work that is already complete. Start with an updated forecast and a list of changes in the business, the owner's circumstances, and planned transactions. Ask the adviser to identify the actual deadlines that apply to each item.

sections.title: Focus on decisions, not a generic deduction list
sections.text: Review owner compensation, capital spending, expense documentation, tax payments, benefits, and pending transactions. Ask why each recommendation fits the specific business and what records are required. Avoid purchasing something solely because it appears on a year-end checklist.

sections.title: Prepare the filing handoff
sections.text: Assign responsibility for final financial statements, payroll reporting, asset schedules, and missing documents. Keep a record of elections and decisions so the filing team can connect the plan to the return. Schedule an early follow-up for unresolved items.

checklist: Updated forecast and payment history
Planned purchases, transactions, and owner payments
Benefits and payroll items needing review
A document and implementation list with named owners
questions: Which decisions have a deadline before year-end?
What has actually been implemented?
What does the filing team still need?
